name: Nathan Johnson
contest: Texas Attorney General — Democratic Primary, March 3, 2026
incumbencyStatus: challenger (current state senator, SD-16, Dallas; not incumbent AG)

priorRoles: Litigator and mediator, Thompson Coburn LLP (Dallas) — trial litigation and dispute resolution
Co-founded law firm specializing in business disputes
Pro-bono work: Human Rights Initiative of North Texas (immigrant legal representation)
Composer: Dragon Ball Z anime musical scores; classical works
biography.education: B.S. Physics, University of Arizona; J.D., University of Texas at Austin School of Law
biography.background: Born February 12, 1968. Upset incumbent Republican Don Huffines by 8 points in 2018 to become the first Democrat to represent SD-16 in over three decades. Re-elected 2020, 2022, 2024. Won a contested 2024 Democratic primary against State Rep. Victoria Neave Criado (who accused him of being too moderate on immigration) with ~60% of the vote. Political scientists describe his voting record as 'nearly indistinguishable from most other Democrats in the Texas Senate.' Represents ~1 million constituents in rapidly growing and diversifying Dallas County. Has authored ~433 bills and passed 134–135 into law across healthcare, electric grid, government transparency, criminal justice, housing, and environmental protection.
biography.fundraising: $750,000 cash on hand (reported); leading Democratic primary polls at ~25%

campaignWebsite.notes: WebFetch unavailable; positions reconstructed from web searches returning summaries and quotes from nathanfortexas.com/priorities, /meet-nathan, /endorsements, /public-health, plus syndicated coverage of the same pages.

statedPositions.quote: The Attorney General is the chief law enforcement officer of Texas, and the office should be protecting consumers, cracking down on fraud, and partnering with law enforcement — not defending illegal power grabs or serving corrupt politicians.
statedPositions.notes: Primary campaign framing; repeated across all campaign materials and interviews.

statedPositions.quote: Texas has laws to protect consumers and promote competition among businesses, and as Attorney General, I will enforce them against businesses who engage in price gouging, consumer scams, and unfair competition.
statedPositions.notes: Signals active enforcement of existing consumer protection and antitrust laws, including Medicaid fraud investigation.

statedPositions.quote: I have great discretion in enforcement powers. The attorney general actually isn't the front-line enforcer on many things, but I do have discretion as to how to use the resources. There are priorities and there are lesser priorities.
statedPositions.notes: Explicitly said he would NOT enforce SB 8 (2025 transgender bathroom/spaces bill), citing enforcement discretion.

statedPositions.quote: I'm not going to defend unconstitutional laws. I've sworn an oath to the Constitution over and over again since I was 18 years old, and that continues today. The dividing line isn't my personal ideology — it's whether a law is constitutional.

The Texas border is 1,254 miles long, and it needs to be secure and safe from drug smuggling, human trafficking, and all forms of cross-border criminal enterprise. [But] Americans should reject 'shock and awe' border policy and tactics that violate the U.S. Constitution... The Attorney General has a role to play: assisting with federal enforcement as appropriate, and blocking federal actions when they go too far.
statedPositions.notes: Moderate framing: supports border security but opposes constitutional violations; would both assist AND check federal enforcement.

statedPositions.quote: I'm not going to use the office to do what either the Biden or Trump administrations say, but rather to ensure that everybody knows the rules and that everybody follows the rules, and then if you don't follow the rules, there's consequences.
statedPositions.notes: CBS Texas interview. States independence from both parties' executive pressure.

statedPositions.quote: I will use the power of the Office to defend — and where possible restore — the individual rights and freedoms we have worked so hard to establish, and to uphold the rule of law and honor the Constitution.
statedPositions.notes: Context includes reproductive rights, LGBTQ rights rolled back in TX.

sources: Texas Right to Life 2019 scorecard PDF
NBC DFW, Texas Tribune, and KHOU vote reporting
votingRecord.legislativeSummary: Authored ~433 bills since 2019; passed 134–135 into law across healthcare, electric grid, government transparency, criminal justice, housing, environmental protection, and AI/data privacy.

keyVotes.bill: HB 1927 — Permitless Carry (87th Legislature, 2021)
keyVotes.vote: No (inferred: all 13 No votes were Democrats; Johnson explicitly opposed and criticized passage)
keyVotes.notes: Johnson stated he 'would never have dreamed it would come out of the House.' In his 87th Legislature blog: 'How did it make sense for the Legislature to pass legislation that was opposed by a supermajority of the voting population?' Senate passed 18-13 along party lines. NRA grade: F. Vote No confirmed by party-line count and multiple statements.

keyVotes.bill: SB 8 (88th Legislature) — Education savings account (ESA) voucher program
keyVotes.notes: Voted against ESA/voucher bill in the regular session.

keyVotes.bill: HB 100 (as amended with ESA provision) — ESA voucher
keyVotes.notes: Voted against ESA voucher program in second attempt.

keyVotes.bill: SB 1 (88th Legislature, 3rd Called Special Session, Oct 2023) — ESA voucher program
keyVotes.notes: Third attempt at vouchers — Johnson voted No each time. Explicit quote: 'No. I will continue to work hard to stop the turnover of public education to the private sector.' Bill passed Senate but died in the House.

keyVotes.bill: Teacher pay amendment ($10,000 raise) (88th Legislature)
keyVotes.notes: Supported teacher pay raise; ATPE-backed vote.

keyVotes.bill: SB 321 (2021) — Defined-contribution plan for new state employees
keyVotes.notes: Opposed converting state employee retirement from defined-benefit to defined-contribution pension. Protects public employee benefits.

keyVotes.bill: Critical race theory / social studies curriculum restriction (2nd Special Session 2021)
keyVotes.notes: Voted against restricting social studies curriculum and banning CRT-associated concepts in schools.

keyVotes.bill: SB 4 (88th Legislature, 3rd Special Session 2023) — Human smuggling penalties / immigration enforcement
keyVotes.notes: CONTESTED VOTE. Voted yes on bill increasing mandatory minimum for human smuggling to 10 years. Passed 29-2 (only 2 Democrats voted No). 2024 primary challenger Neave Criado attacked this vote as too moderate on immigration; Johnson defended it as anti-trafficking. Conflicts with his general rehabilitation/reform sentencing direction.

keyVotes.bill: SB 1296 (2021) — Texas insurance / Medicaid access expansion
keyVotes.notes: Amended Texas insurance law to provide private health coverage to ~350,000 previously uninsured low-income Texans. Johnson's landmark healthcare bill; Medicaid expansion workaround via private insurance mechanism.

keyVotes.bill: SB 195 — Live Well Texas Program (1115 Waiver Medicaid expansion)
keyVotes.notes: Full Medicaid expansion by 1115 waiver under ACA (90-10 federal-state match); would cover ~1 million Texans. Repeatedly filed by Johnson; blocked by Republican-controlled Senate. D Magazine describes him as 'the state's leading voice on Medicaid expansion.'

keyVotes.bill: Fentanyl testing strip decriminalization (SB 623 and companion, 88th Legislature)
keyVotes.notes: Bipartisan bill with Republican Sen. Bob Hall. Passed. Harm-reduction approach: decriminalizes test strips that prevent overdose deaths.

keyVotes.bill: Teen mental health services market creation (87th Legislature, 2021)
keyVotes.notes: Created new market for teen mental-health services. Cited as notable bipartisan success in his own 87th Legislature recap.

keyVotes.bill: Palliative care definition expansion (passed)
keyVotes.notes: Expanded palliative care access in state law.

keyVotes.bill: SB 53 — Hemp-derived THC regulatory framework (89th Legislature Special Session, July 2025)
keyVotes.notes: Establishes regulatory rather than criminal framework for hemp-derived THC products. Filed July 2025 in special session.

keyVotes.bill: SB 54 — Marijuana decriminalization and expungement (89th Legislature Special Session, July 2025)
keyVotes.notes: Decriminalize possession of up to 2 oz, allow limited home cultivation, create expungement path for past low-level convictions. Filed after his AG announcement; legislative outcome pending.

keyVotes.bill: SB 2835 — Single-staircase apartment buildings (89th Legislature, 2025)
keyVotes.notes: Allows municipalities to authorize single-stairway apartment buildings up to 6 stories ('gentle density'). Grants municipalities discretion — not a state preemption of local zoning. Part of first-day 89th Legislature housing package.

keyVotes.bill: Housing construction regulatory barrier removal (89th Legislature first-day filing)
keyVotes.notes: First-day legislation filing (November 12, 2024) to remove regulatory blocks on construction of promising new housing forms. Framed by Johnson as 'physical infrastructure.'

keyVotes.bill: Texas Power Promise / Winter Storm Uri grid reform (87th Legislature, 2021)
keyVotes.notes: Required PUC to develop $1.8B program for backup power at critical community facilities. Secured nearly $2B total for backup power statewide. Explicitly preserved renewable energy resources within grid reforms against Republican proposals to disadvantage renewables.

keyVotes.bill: Texas Virtual Power Plant pilot (2023)
keyVotes.notes: Authored bill kickstarting Texas virtual power plant pilot as part of ERCOT grid reliability work.

keyVotes.bill: ERCOT board governance — opposed politicizing ERCOT
keyVotes.notes: Johnson raised concerns about replacing independent ERCOT experts with political appointees: 'We represent to the public that ERCOT is an independent agency, and yet under the various options... we're appointing members politically.'

keyVotes.bill: Polluter penalty increases (multiple sessions)
keyVotes.notes: Passed legislation increasing penalties on polluters. Stated goal: 'continue the trend of lowering carbon pollution.'

keyVotes.bill: Corporate tax abatement reform
keyVotes.notes: Rewrote standards to prevent waste and abuse of business tax abatements; made it harder for businesses to exploit tax incentives. Anti-corporate-welfare angle.

keyVotes.bill: AI scam / data privacy consumer protection (passed)
keyVotes.notes: Passed legislation protecting consumers from AI scams and invasions of data privacy.

keyVotes.bill: SB 45 — Abortion travel ban prohibition
keyVotes.notes: Filed SB 45 to prohibit abortion travel bans in Texas.

keyVotes.bill: SB 78 — Medication abortion legalization
keyVotes.notes: Only legislator in Texas to introduce medication abortion legalization bill after Texas abortion ban. Did not pass Republican-controlled Senate.

keyVotes.bill: SB 79 — Nullify 1925 pre-Roe abortion prosecution statute
keyVotes.notes: Filed to nullify 1925 law allowing prosecution of women who obtain abortions.

keyVotes.bill: SB 291 — Out-of-state abortion travel protection
keyVotes.notes: Filed to protect from prosecution anyone who helps a woman travel out of state to obtain an abortion.

keyVotes.bill: Anti-abortion bills — multiple (86th–88th Legislatures)
keyVotes.notes: Documented No votes: medication abortion ban (7 weeks), criminal penalties for providers, 6-week abortion ban, charter school restriction on abortion providers. 100% Reproductive Freedom for All (NARAL) lifetime score.

keyVotes.bill: Property tax relief package (88th Legislature, 2023)
keyVotes.notes: Supported bipartisan $16.5B property tax cut. Stated: 'We're doing something that's popular, we're doing something that provides genuine tax relief for people' but noted it 'could require us to make some difficult decisions in the future.' No Democrats voted against it. Constituent-service vote, not ideological low-tax position.

keyVotes.bill: SBOE veto power amendment (preserving elected State Board of Education oversight)
keyVotes.notes: Voted to preserve elected State Board of Education's veto power over rules adopted by appointed State Board for Educator Certification. ATPE-supported.

keyExchanges.quote: Restoring integrity and accountability to an office that has been turned into a laughingstock... The Attorney General is the chief law enforcement officer of Texas.
keyExchanges.notes: Most structured interview: direct Q&A with all three Democratic AG primary candidates.

keyExchanges.quote: He would focus on restoring some of the agency's less prominent obligations, like investigating Medicaid fraud and enforcing consumer protection laws.
keyExchanges.notes: Signals continued Medicaid investment as policy value via enforcement focus.

keyExchanges.quote: We need somebody as the chief legal officer of this state who understands state government, who, yes, can work with Republicans — that's how I managed to pass 135 bills — who, yes, can stand up to authority.
keyExchanges.notes: Emphasizes pragmatic bipartisan approach; 135 bills passed with Republican cooperation in a GOP-supermajority legislature.

keyExchanges.quote: I'm not going to use the office to do what either the Biden or Trump administrations say, but rather to ensure that everybody knows the rules and that everybody follows the rules, and then if you don't follow the rules, there's consequences.
keyExchanges.notes: Positions himself as independent of both federal political pressures.

keyExchanges.quote: The legislature does not have the right to enforce unconstitutional laws, and I would not enforce unconstitutional laws.
keyExchanges.notes: Distinguishes between laws he must defend (constitutional) vs. those he won't (unconstitutional).

keyExchanges.quote: Johnson cited last year's Senate Bill (SB) 8, prohibiting biological males from women's private spaces, as legislation he would not seek to enforce.
keyExchanges.notes: Explicit example of enforcement discretion — would decline to enforce the 2025 transgender bathroom bill on resource/priority grounds.

keyExchanges.quote: I have great discretion in enforcement powers. The attorney general actually isn't the front-line enforcer on many things, but I do have discretion as to how to use the resources. There are priorities and there are lesser priorities.
keyExchanges.notes: Key framing of how he would use prosecutorial discretion as AG.

keyExchanges.quote: The framers of the Texas Constitution wanted the attorney general to be part of the executive branch, independently elected by the voters to act as a check to the concentration of power and the abuse of power, wherever it is in government, in the marketplace and on the streets.
keyExchanges.notes: Philosophical framing of AG as independent check on power.

keyExchanges.topic: Paxton failure to challenge Trump on education funding
keyExchanges.quote: Why didn't we join that suit [against Trump's education funding freeze]? Because [Paxton] doesn't want to challenge the Trump administration.
keyExchanges.notes: Signals willingness to sue the Trump administration where Texas education funding interests are at stake.

keyExchanges.quote: I hate to be too partisan about this stuff, and I have a record for working well across the aisle. But at the moment, there's such a pull from the attorney general's office to run it as a political machine for the far right.
keyExchanges.notes: Bipartisan rhetorical framing for AG race. Note: contrast with YCT 22/100 and NRA F — this is campaign positioning, not a moderate Senate voting record.

keyExchanges.quote: It has 'become such an ideological play pen for Ken Paxton' and if elected, the focus would shift from Republican talking points to basic functions of the Attorney General's Office, such as consumer protection and child support.
keyExchanges.notes: Consumer protection and family services enforcement framed as proper core AG function.

keyExchanges.quote: How did it make sense for the Legislature to pass legislation that was opposed by a supermajority of the voting population? [regarding permitless gun carry]
keyExchanges.notes: Opposed permitless carry on democratic responsiveness grounds. Confirms No vote by statement and party-line split.

keyExchanges.summary: Praised bipartisan work on teen mental health and COVID liability; criticized partisan overreach on guns, SB 1, and other 87th session bills.
keyExchanges.notes: Tier 2 self-authored source; useful for governing philosophy.

evidenceSummary.characterProfile: Pragmatic progressive in the Texas Democratic mold — strongly liberal on healthcare access, education, gun safety, reproductive rights, and environment, but with a track record of working across the aisle (134–135 bills passed in a GOP-supermajority legislature). His 2024 primary challenger attacked him as too moderate on immigration, and his Yes vote on SB 4 (human smuggling mandatory minimums) is the most significant rightward deviation from standard Democratic sentencing positions. His 2026 AG campaign emphasizes institutional restoration, rule of law, and enforcement discretion — appropriate to the office — rather than sweeping policy change.
scoringNotes: Johnson has a 7-year Texas Senate record providing strong Tier 1 evidence on the highest-salience axes. Score from the record, not from the institutionalist AG campaign framing.
The 'I hate to be too partisan' rhetoric is for a statewide general election audience. The voting record (YCT 22-30/100, NRA F, 100% NARAL, three voucher No votes) is the reliable signal.

Texas context: no state income tax limits econ_tax_structure applicability. Energy policy must account for ERCOT grid reliability context — Johnson's 'balance renewables with traditional energy' is a Texas grid reality statement, not ideological moderation on climate.
SB 4 (human smuggling mandatory minimums) is a meaningful exception on justice_sentencing_goals. Do not smooth it away. Score that axis with the exception noted.
Do not score housing_transport_priority or climate_permitting — no evidence exists. Do not manufacture neutral 5s.
